# Outsourced / BPO Support

`customer_support.model.outsourced_bpo` · model · parent `—`

> Contacts are handled by a third-party provider working to a contract. The provider is a business, not a department: it optimises what its contract measures, which is almost always cost per contact, handled volume, average handle time and adherence. None of those is the customer's outcome, and the gap between them is not a vendor quality problem — it is the specification. Whatever is written into the statement of work is what arrives, precisely and only, and every complaint about a BPO that is not traceable to a clause is a complaint about the clause that was never written. . The defining structural fact is a commercial boundary drawn straight through the middle of the resolution motion. The agents handling contacts do not have the source, the roadmap, the incident channel or a relationship with an engineer, and they are frequently not permitted to see account value or contract terms. So the branch cannot own root cause — not because the people are less capable, but because the organisation that sees the evidence first has been placed outside the organisation that can act on it. The provider notices a pattern in week one, has no channel, no permission and no incentive to raise it, and the client discovers the same defect a quarter later through a churn conversation. . Second: knowledge is the interface, and it is a hard ceiling. A BPO agent can be exactly as good as the runbook and no better, because product intuition is what tenure buys and tenure is what this staffing model does not have. An underwritten knowledge base does not produce slightly worse handling here; it produces a transfer rate, and the transfers land back on the client, who then pays twice for the contact they outsourced. . Third: attrition is structural, not incidental. Every quality improvement decays at the rate the provider's floor turns over, which means training is a recurring operating line and not a project with an end date. A quality programme that assumes a stable cohort will report a gain, then report the same gain again next year, and never compound. . What an operator carries over wrongly from an in-house team: informal escalation. In-house, a hard ticket is solved by walking over to someone. Across this boundary the same act is a contractual event with a queue, a hand-back and an argument about who owns the clock — and the context that walked over in a conversation now has to be written down or it is lost. The single largest hidden cost of outsourcing is re-diagnosis at the client after a hand-back that carried no evidence.


## Characteristics

|  |  |
|---|---|
| requester | unchanged from whatever motion is being outsourced — the customer usually does not know they are talking to a different company, and finding out is itself a support event |
| typical_resolution_hours | 12 |
| volume_shape | high volume, low-to-moderate complexity by contract; the tail is explicitly out of scope and hands back, so the shape at the provider is flatter than the shape of the real demand |
| staffing_model | contracted provider FTEs on a scripted tier one, with a hand-back path to the client for anything outside the runbook |
| coverage | whatever was purchased, usually broader and cheaper than in-house — extended hours are the most common reason this model is chosen at all |
| automation_level | moderate to high on the provider side, because deflection and macro coverage are how the provider protects its own margin |
| primary_channels | `phone`, `chat`, `email`, `ticket_portal` |
| notes | Watch the incentive on scope. The provider is paid per contact handled and penalised for hand-backs, so there is steady pressure to close things that were not resolved — and the metric that catches it is the reopen and the repeat contact, neither of which appears in the provider's own reporting by default. If the client does not measure repeat contact independently, this branch will report improving performance while getting worse.  |

## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.knowledge_article`

Requires `audience`, `accuracy_state`, `last_verified_at`


> Two audiences that a single-org branch can blur and this one cannot: the customer-facing article and the agent-facing runbook are different documents with different failure modes. A runbook that is wrong produces a confidently wrong answer at scale from people with no basis to doubt it; a customer article that is wrong at least meets a reader who knows their own system. Conflating them is how a provider gets blamed for the client's documentation.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.escalation`

Requires `context_handed_over`, `context_package`, `receiving_owner_ref`, `reason`


> A hand-back across an org boundary with no evidence package is a re-diagnosis paid for twice. This is the attribute set that decides whether outsourcing is cheaper than in-house, and it is usually left optional because the cost lands on the other party. Make context_handed_over mandatory and the arrangement's economics change measurably; leave it optional and the provider's incentive is to hand back early and thin.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.entitlement`

Requires `plan`, `entitled_channels`, `coverage_hours`


> The provider frequently cannot see account value, and often should not. That is a real privacy and commercial constraint and not an oversight — but it means severity and priority are being decided blind to the one fact that most often inverts them. The workable answer is a derived tier pushed down to the provider rather than raw ARR pushed down; the unworkable answer, which is the common one, is to let the provider infer importance from how angry the customer sounds.


## Extends `customer_support.obj.core.ticket`

Requires `team`, `assignee_ref`, `reopen_count`, `escalation_ref`


> `team` is doing unusual work in this branch: it records which side of the commercial boundary the ticket is currently on, which is the single most important fact about it and is not derivable from the assignee. `reopen_count` is the client's only independent instrument against a provider paid for closures.
